opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic object we start with is the local learning coefficient, the LLC, which comes out of singular learning theory. Roughly, it measures the effective dimensionality or complexity of a model at a particular point in parameter space: how many directions really matter for the loss, as opposed to directions you can wiggle without changing much. That's a single number for the whole model, which is useful but pretty coarse.

The refined LLC splits that number up in two ways. The first is what we call the *weight-refined* LLC. Instead of measuring the complexity across all the parameters, you hold most of the network fixed and only sample over a subset of the weights, say the weights belonging to one particular attention head. That gives you something like "how much complexity does this head contribute," or "how much structure has this component learned."

The second is the *data-refined* LLC. Instead of measuring loss over the full training distribution, you measure it over a particular slice of data, for example code, or text with lots of nested brackets, or some other subdistribution. Then you can ask how complex this head is with respect to this kind of data specifically.

So in the paper we trained a small two-layer attention-only transformer on a Pile-style language modeling distribution, and we tracked the weight-refined LLC for each head over the course of training. Two things happen. One is *differentiation*: heads that start out looking basically identical develop quite distinct LLC trajectories, and when you cluster heads by those curves, the clusters line up with functional types people already recognized: previous-token heads, induction heads, current-token heads, and some more complex heads we called multigram heads. So the trajectory of the rLLC works as a kind of fingerprint for what a head ends up doing, and you can read it off without already knowing the circuit you're looking for.

The other is *specialization*, which is where the data-refined version comes in. You compare a head's LLC measured on, say, code versus ordinary natural language. If a head's complexity is disproportionately concentrated on code, that suggests it's specializing to that part of the distribution. That's actually how we found a circuit we hadn't anticipated: a head, or a small group of them, that seemed to be dealing with nested brackets, matching open and close parentheses. The data-refined LLC pointed us there first, and then we confirmed it with more traditional interpretability work.

The broader point, for me, is that this gives you a principled, theory-grounded way to ask developmental questions: not just what a component does at the end of training, but when it forms, what it's responding to in the data, and how it differentiates from its neighbors. That fits our larger agenda of developmental interpretability: using the geometry of the loss landscape to locate where and when structure appears, and then zooming in.

r001.rationale: It says to hold most of the network fixed and measure a subset of weights, such as one head’s weights, to estimate that component’s complexity.

r002.rationale: It explains that measuring the data-refined LLC on a slice such as code can reveal specialization to that part of the distribution.

r003.rationale: It says LLC trajectories distinguish heads, including induction heads, and separately describes code-related bracket matching. It does not say code evaluation distinguishes induction heads that previously appeared to perform the same function.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea is that the local learning coefficient is a measure of how much a model's loss changes when you perturb its weights, and the refined version lets you ask that question about a specific subset of the weights, or a specific subset of the data, rather than the whole thing at once.

So concretely, you take a trained model, say a small two-layer attention-only transformer, and instead of computing the learning coefficient over all the parameters, you restrict it to the parameters of a single attention head. And instead of computing it over the full data distribution, you can also restrict it to a particular kind of data, like sequences where a certain token pattern shows up. What you get out is a number that tells you something like: how sensitive is the loss on this data to changes in this head? How much is this head "doing" for this slice of the distribution?

And the reason that's useful is that if a head has really specialized, its refined local learning coefficient will be high on the data it cares about and low elsewhere. So you can scan over heads and over data subsets, and you get a kind of fingerprint for each head. In our work we found that this actually lines up quite well with the structure people had already found by hand with mechanistic interpretability, so you see heads that look like previous-token heads, induction heads, and so on, and they separate out cleanly in terms of which data they have high learning coefficients on.

The other thing that's nice is you can do this over the course of training, not just at the end. So you can watch the per-head learning coefficients change over time, and that lets you see when a head starts to specialize, when it picks up its role, sometimes when two heads trade off and one takes over a function from another. That developmental picture is a lot harder to get from just looking at the final weights.

I should say it's not a replacement for doing the circuit-level analysis. It doesn't tell you the mechanism, it tells you where to look and when something changed. But that's often most of the battle, because the hard part of interpretability is usually narrowing down which pieces of the model matter for what, and this gives you a fairly principled, geometry-based way to do that narrowing.

r001.rationale: It says to restrict the calculation to one head’s parameters, but does not explain that freezing the other weights measures complexity within that component.

r002.rationale: It explains that evaluating on selected data subsets reveals which data a head specializes in.

r003.rationale: It mentions induction heads generally, but does not report that evaluation on code distinguishes heads that previously appeared to perform the same function.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is to localize the measurement in two ways: which parameters you look at, and which data you evaluate them on. So you can restrict attention to the parameters of a particular head, and then measure its local learning coefficient on different kinds of inputs.

The learning coefficient is a measure of local complexity. Roughly, it tells you how constrained those parameters are by the task: how much room is there to perturb them while keeping the loss low? It’s not just counting parameters, because many directions in parameter space can be redundant or leave the behavior unchanged.

To investigate specialization, you might compare ordinary text with data containing repeated patterns. If a head is doing something like induction—using an earlier occurrence of a sequence to predict what comes next—then you’d expect the repeated-pattern data to constrain it differently. Measuring that across heads gives you a kind of profile of which heads are sensitive to which distributions. And measuring it across checkpoints lets you investigate when that specialization develops.

That gives you evidence for a functional interpretation, rather than a complete explanation of the circuit. You’d still want to look at attention patterns and do interventions to check what the head actually does.

r001.rationale: It says to restrict the measurement to a particular head’s parameters, but does not explain that other weights are frozen.

r002.rationale: It explains that comparing measurements across different input distributions, such as ordinary text and repeated-pattern data, can reveal head specialization.

r003.rationale: It discusses repeated-pattern data and induction, but does not report that code evaluation distinguishes induction heads that previously appeared to perform the same function.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is to localize the learning coefficient in two ways: which parameters you allow to vary, and which data you use to evaluate the loss. So you might let just the parameters of one attention head vary, keeping the rest of the model fixed, and then measure its local learning coefficient on different kinds of inputs.

That gives you something like a fingerprint for the head. Rather than just asking how much removing the head hurts performance, you’re asking about the geometry of the loss around its learned parameters—how constrained those parameters are by a particular prediction task. If you do that across heads and across data distributions, you can look for heads that have similar fingerprints, or for changes in those fingerprints during training.

The important caveat is that this doesn’t automatically give you a semantic label like ‘this is an induction head.’ You still need to connect the measurement to behavior, using examples or interventions. But it gives you a way to identify candidate specializations and track when they emerge, without having to start with a complete mechanistic account of what every head is doing.

r001.rationale: It says to vary only one head’s parameters while keeping the rest of the model fixed, then measure the loss geometry around that head’s learned parameters.

r002.rationale: It says to evaluate on different kinds of inputs and data distributions to find differences in attention heads’ fingerprints and candidate specializations.

r003.rationale: It does not mention code evaluation or say that it distinguishes induction heads that previously appeared to perform the same function.
